stages.name: Beyond the network
stages.desc: No lasting Phoenician presence known yet

stages.name: Source of raw materials
stages.desc: Metals drew the ships here above all else

stages.name: Trading partner
stages.desc: Other peoples' lands, ports and markets

stages.name: Phoenician homeland
stages.desc: The mother cities of the Levantine coast

states.name: Cyprus
timeline: Phoenician Kition, the nearest overseas town, stands beside the copper of the Troodos hills
Copper aboard the Bajo de la Campana ship may include Cypriot metal

states.name: Israel
timeline: Philistine Ashkelon, Israel and Judah trade with the Phoenicians; Akko and Dor are busy ports
Esarhaddon's treaty names Akko and Dor among the ports open to Tyre's ships
Nebuchadnezzar destroys Ashkelon, a major wine producer of the southern coast

states.name: Lebanon
timeline: Tyre, Sidon and Byblos: the home ports; kilns at Sarepta turn out torpedo-shaped jars
Luli, king of Tyre and Sidon, escapes by ship before Sennacherib's army reaches the coast
Esarhaddon's treaty with Tyre's king sets terms for its ships and ports
Babylon begins its long siege of Tyre, by tradition thirteen years
The siege ends; Tyre survives, but no longer leads the western trade

states.name: Spain
timeline: Silver draws the ships to Huelva and to the Phoenician town of Gadir (Cádiz)
Two small boats sink at Mazarrón; one carries almost three tonnes of lead-rich litharge
A merchantman with tin, copper, lead ore and ivory strikes the Bajo de la Campana reef
With Tyre weakened, Gadir and the southern towns carry on in their own right
Toscanos and La Fonteta have shrunk or been abandoned as the old network reshapes

states.name: Tunisia
timeline: Carthage and Utica; torpedo jars like those of the deep wrecks reach Carthage
Jars made around Carthage or Utica sail on the Xlendi ship
Carthage emerges as the leading Phoenician city of the west

states.name: Italy
timeline: Pithekoussai and Sant'Imbenia: Phoenicians trade with Euboean Greeks and Sardinians
Phoenician towns hold Sardinia's southern coast and western Sicily: Sulcis, Tharros, Motya
Grinding stones from Pantelleria and jars of Tyrrhenian style sail on the Xlendi ship

states.name: Egypt
timeline: A market for Levantine wine and cedar; Stager's preferred goal for the wine ships, though disputed
Greek traders settle at Naukratis in the Delta, a new rival in the Egyptian market
Herodotus says Pharaoh Necho sent Phoenician crews to sail around Africa; scholars are divided

states.name: N. Cyprus
timeline: Cypriot kingdoms such as Salamis trade with Kition; drawn with the rest of the island

states.name: Cyprus U.N. Buffer Zone
timeline: Part of Cyprus; drawn with the rest of the island

states.name: Malta
timeline: Phoenician traders may call here, but no settlement is known yet
Phoenician burials appear around Rabat and Mtarfa by about this date
A cargo ship sinks off Xlendi on Gozo, carrying jars probably made on Malta

events.title: Tanit and Elissa sink
events.text: Two wine ships go down upright about sixty kilometres offshore; a US Navy submarine spots them in 1997, and Ballard and Stager survey them in 1999.

events.title: Tyre, the great port
events.text: Tyre is the leading Phoenician harbour, and the excavators' candidate for the wine ships' home port.

events.title: Sarepta's jar kilns
events.text: Kilns at Sarepta make torpedo-shaped jars like those on the deep wrecks, perhaps for filling at Tyre.

events.title: Ashkelon's rival claim
events.text: Some scholars place the jars' origin on the southern Levantine coast, probably near Ashkelon, rather than at Tyre.

events.title: Stager's Egyptian goal
events.text: Stager argued the wine was bound for the Nile Delta, though no eighth-century torpedo jars are documented in Egypt.

events.title: Jars reach Carthage
events.text: Torpedo jars of this type do reach Carthage, a Tyrian colony whose earliest levels date to about 835–800 BC.

events.title: Huelva's silver trade
events.text: Phoenicians have traded for generations at Huelva, the outlet for the silver of the Río Tinto.

events.title: Gadir
events.text: The Phoenician town at Cádiz stands beyond Gibraltar, the gateway to Atlantic metals.

events.title: Kition
events.text: Phoenician Kition on Cyprus is the nearest overseas town, close to the island's copper.

events.title: Sant'Imbenia
events.text: Phoenician traders and Nuragic Sardinians exchange goods here, where local workshops make transport jars.

events.title: Pithekoussai
events.text: Euboean Greeks, Phoenicians and local people share this trading island in the Bay of Naples.

events.title: Sulcis
events.text: A Phoenician town stands on Sardinia's south-west coast, on the sea road to Spain.

events.title: Toscanos
events.text: Phoenicians settle on the coast east of Málaga, one of a string of small towns.

events.title: Motya
events.text: A Phoenician settlement grows on a small island off western Sicily, facing Carthage.

events.title: Luli flees by ship
events.text: Luli, king of Tyre and Sidon, escapes to Cyprus before Sennacherib, whose palace reliefs picture Phoenician round-hulled ships.

events.title: Phoenicians on Malta
events.text: Tombs around Rabat and Mtarfa show a settled Phoenician presence on the island by about this date.

events.title: Lixus
events.text: Phoenician traders work this Atlantic port in Morocco, one proposed source of the ivory found in later wrecks.

events.title: Pantelleria's querns
events.text: Basalt grinding stones are quarried in the island's north-west for clients across the central Mediterranean.

events.title: The Xlendi ship sinks
events.text: A cargo ship goes down off Gozo between 700 and 650 BC, in water a hundred and ten metres deep.

events.title: A treaty of ports
events.text: Esarhaddon's treaty with Tyre names Akko and Dor, and claims the cargo of Tyrian ships wrecked in Assyrian waters.

events.title: Ibiza
events.text: Ancient tradition dates a Phoenician foundation on Ibiza to about now; it later appears as a possible goal of the Bajo de la Campana ship.

events.title: Rachgoun
events.text: A Phoenician outpost on this islet off Algeria yields a jug much like those made on Malta.

events.title: Abul
events.text: Phoenician traders build a post on the Sado estuary in Portugal, reaching further up the Atlantic coast.

events.title: Colaeus off course
events.text: Herodotus says a storm drove the Samian trader Colaeus through Gibraltar to rich Tartessos, a reminder of what storms can do.

events.title: The Mazarrón boats
events.text: Two boats of about eight metres sink close inshore, sometime between about 625 and 570 BC.

events.title: Lead of Mazarrón
events.text: The litharge aboard came from the hills behind the bay, where silver was refined from lead ores.

events.title: Naukratis
events.text: Greek traders gain a base in the Nile Delta, new competitors in the Egyptian market.

events.title: Bajo de la Campana
events.text: A merchantman, dated to the late seventh or early sixth century BC, strikes a reef off La Manga.

events.title: Tin of the north-west
events.text: Tin in the Bajo de la Campana cargo has been attributed to Galicia or northern Portugal.

events.title: La Fonteta
events.text: This Phoenician town on the Segura estuary is one proposed destination of the Bajo de la Campana ship.

events.title: Ashkelon destroyed
events.text: Nebuchadnezzar destroys the city, ending a major wine port of the southern Levantine coast.

events.title: Necho's African voyage
events.text: Herodotus says Phoenician crews sailed around Africa for Pharaoh Necho; no physical evidence exists, and scholars are divided.

events.title: Massalia
events.text: Phocaean Greeks found a colony at Marseille, opening a rival trade route in the western Mediterranean.

events.title: Ezekiel's trade list
events.text: A prophecy against Tyre lists its trade: Tarshish's silver, iron, tin and lead, ivory, wine, and human beings.

events.title: Siege of Tyre begins
events.text: Nebuchadnezzar's army besieges the island city, by tradition for thirteen years.

events.title: Siege of Tyre ends
events.text: Tyre survives on terms, its leadership of the western trade much diminished.

events.title: Gadir on its own
events.text: The western towns increasingly trade without their mother city; the date is only a rough marker.

events.title: Carthage rises
events.text: Carthage emerges as the leading Phoenician city of the western Mediterranean.

events.title: Toscanos declines
events.text: Towns around Málaga shrink or are abandoned as the western network reshapes.

events.title: La Fonteta abandoned
events.text: The Phoenician town on the Segura estuary is deserted by about the middle of the century.

events.title: Kerkouane
events.text: A Punic town grows on Cape Bon, as Carthage's own coast fills with settlements.

chartNote: Share of the area of the mapped countries, by each one's main role in the Phoenician network. This is a simplification: regions are today's boundaries, Phoenician towns held only stretches of coast, and Egypt's size swings the shares. Spain's change in 573 BC is a rough marker, not a sharp switch. The homeland also ran north into Syria, and Morocco and Portugal are shown by events only.
